title: Dilucidationes super methodo elegantissima, qua illustris de la Grange usus est in integranda aequatione differentiali dx/√X = dy/√Y

deep.reconstruction:
Setting. E506 explains Lagrange's method for the Euler addition equation dx/√X + dy/√Y = 0, where X and Y are the same quartic A+Bx+Cx²+Dx³+Ex⁴ written in x and in y. Earlier (§58) the general integral is given in two equivalent forms:
(i) [2A+B(x+y)+2Cxy+Dxy(x+y)+2Ex²y² − 2√(XY)]/(x−y)² = Δ;
(ii) (√X−√Y)/(x−y) = √(Δ + D(x+y) + E(x+y)²).

The paradox (§§57–58). Take X a perfect square, √X = R = a+bx+cx² (so A=a², B=2ab, C=2ac+b², D=2bc, E=c²). Form (i) collapses identically to Δ = −2ac. It carries no information about the integral of dx/R + dy/S = 0.

§59 (this page). Euler remarks that this indeterminacy is of a new kind. It is not 0/0 and not ∞−∞, and he does not recall meeting such a case. It occurs exactly when X and Y become squares. The remedy is to let X and Y differ from squares by an infinitesimal.

§60. Set X = R² + α and Y = S² + α, with S = a+by+cy². Then A = a²+α and the other coefficients are unchanged. To first order, √X = R + α/(2R) and √Y = S + α/(2S).

§61. Insert this into form (ii):
• √X − √Y = R − S − α(R−S)/(2RS).
• R − S = b(x−y) + c(x²−y²), so (R−S)/(x−y) = b + cp, with p = x+y.

Next page (completing the argument).
• The equation becomes (b+cp)(1 − α/(2RS)) = √(Δ + 2bcp + c²p²).
• Squaring to first order gives b² − α(b+cp)²/(RS) = Δ.
• At α = 0 this forces Δ = b², the trivial identity. So the arbitrary constant must itself be perturbed: Δ = b² − αΓ.
• The result is the genuine integral (b + c(x+y))² = Γ·RS.

In modern terms: a one-parameter family of first integrals F_α degenerates to a constant at α = 0. The true first integral is the first-order coefficient (F_α − F_0)/α, i.e. ∂F/∂α at α = 0. Geometrically, the elliptic curve w² = X degenerates to a rational one, and the elliptic addition law degenerates to the multiplicative (or additive) group law.

Check of the final result. Write R = c(x−r1)(x−r2), M = (x−r1)(y−r1), N = (x−r2)(y−r2). Then M − N = (r2−r1)(x+y−r1−r2), so (b+c(x+y))²/(RS) = (k + 1/k − 2)/(r1−r2)² with k = M/N. Since k = const is exactly the logarithmic integral of dx/R + dy/S = 0, the result is correct.

Check for c = 0: the result gives (a+bx)(a+by) = const, also correct.
errors: None on this page: the expansions √X ≈ R + α/(2R), the first-order difference √X−√Y = R−S−α(R−S)/(2RS), and (R−S)/(x−y) = b + c(x+y) are all correct.
§57 (previous page) correctly yields Δ = −2ac, since the numerator equals −2ac(x−y)².
On the next page, the fraction RS/(b−cp)² in §63 is a misprint for RS/(b+cp)².

ideas.what: Recognition of a new type of analytic indeterminacy: a general integral formula that becomes an identity (the constant is no longer arbitrary) when the radicand is a perfect square, distinct from 0/0 or ∞−∞
ideas.modern_name: Degeneration of a family of first integrals / loss of the integration constant in a degenerate limit
ideas.usually_credited_to: No standard attribution; part of the general theory of degenerations
ideas.where_published: E506 itself (Nova Acta Acad. Sci. Petrop. 1780 volume, published 1784; Opera Omnia I.21)

ideas.what: Resolution by infinitesimal perturbation X = R² + α together with rescaling of the arbitrary constant Δ = b² − αΓ, i.e. taking the first-order coefficient in α of the degenerate integral
ideas.modern_name: Derivative of a parametrized first integral with respect to the parameter at a degenerate value (first-order deformation / renormalization of the constant)
ideas.usually_credited_to: General folklore; Euler used analogous limiting arguments, e.g. repeated roots in linear ODEs
ideas.where_published: E506 §§59–62; analogous limiting devices in Euler's work on linear differential equations with equal roots (unsure of exact item)

ideas.what: Algebraic integral (b+c(x+y))² = Γ(a+bx+cx²)(a+by+cy²) of dx/R + dy/S = 0, obtained as the degenerate limit of the elliptic addition theorem
ideas.modern_name: Degeneration of the elliptic-curve addition law to the multiplicative group law (Möbius/cross-ratio invariance)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical; implicit in Euler and Lagrange, standard in the theory of degenerate elliptic curves

missed.claim: Euler explicitly isolates a general principle: when a family of first integrals collapses at a parameter value, the integration constant must be perturbed with the parameter, and the first-order term gives the true integral. He also says he had never met such a case. This is an early, explicitly flagged instance of what is now done by differentiating a family of invariants with respect to a deformation parameter. It is probably known to E506 commentators but rarely cited as such.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical: it documents Euler's conscious recognition of degeneration phenomena in integrable addition laws. This is a minor point for the history of degenerations of elliptic curves.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a correct and nicely motivated perturbation argument resolving a degeneration of Lagrange's integral. The idea is elegant but elementary from a modern standpoint, and the paper is published and known. At most it is a minor historiographical point about Euler's explicit awareness of degenerate limits.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image; no substantive corrections. Long-s forms (ſ) and 'vſu', 'obtuliſſe' are faithful.
§61 formula: the image shows (√X−√Y)/(x−y) = √(Δ + D(x+y) + E(x+y)²), as transcribed.
